WarningContributors: edit the directory, run the generator



appbay init seeds from the embedded definitions in packages/core/src/system-apps.ts, not from the system-apps/ directory. The definitions are compiled into the binary so that seeding does not depend on filesystem paths relative to the source tree, which are unavailable in a bun-compiled binary.
system-apps/ is the authored source, and a generator produces the embedded file from it. The workflow is three steps:
# 1. edit the app definition
vim system-apps/caddy/config/Caddyfile
# 2. regenerate the embedded copy
node scripts/generate-system-apps.mjs
# 3. commit BOTH
packages/core/src/__tests__/system-apps-sync.test.ts fails the build if the committed generated file is not what the generator would produce right now, so a forgotten step 2 cannot reach main.
⚠️ The generated file is committed rather than built on demand, because appbay init must seed system apps from a single compiled binary with no source tree present.






NoteWhy this matters historically



Before the generator, these were two hand-maintained copies with nothing between them. They drifted to 8 differing files and 2 apps that existed only as embedded strings — and it cost the default ingress: a depends_on: [socket-proxy] left in the Traefik definition after socket-proxy was deleted, which makes Compose reject the entire project rather than skip the service.

title: Core Concepts
section: What Appbay is and is not
text:
What Appbay is and is not
Appbay is a centralized control plane for Docker Compose apps. It adds ingress routing, authentication, secret management, and lifecycle orchestration on top of standard compose files — without modifying the upstream compose.
It is not a service mesh. There are no per-app sidecar proxies, no east-west traffic interception, no mTLS between containers, and no distributed tracing injection. Cross-cutting concerns (routing, auth, secrets) are handled by shared centralized services:

Traefik or Caddy handles all HTTP routing and TLS termination (one instance, not one per app)
Caddy Security handles authentication and authorization for the Caddy edge (one instance, not one per app)
The secrets vault resolves secrets at deploy time and injects them via process environment or file mounts

When your app needs authentication, Appbay generates Caddy Security authorization policies and injects Remote-User/Remote-Email/Remote-Groups headers — it doesn’t inject a proxy container next to your app.
This centralized approach means deploying 30 apps doesn’t create 60 containers. Your compose files stay unmodified. Your apps start and stop independently of the control plane (in default mode).

title: Core Concepts
text:
The compiler pipeline
When you run appbay up, the compiler transforms your app definitions into runnable Compose files, then deploys them:





flowchart LR
    A[Discover + Parse] --> B[Upstream transform]
    B --> C[Resolve variables]
    C --> D[Select overlays]
    D --> E[Apply traits]
    E --> F[Render]
    F --> G[Plan/Diff]
    G --> H[docker compose up]






The pipeline runs in two phases. For each discovered app, stages run in this order:

Discover – Scan etc/apps/ for directories with docker-compose.yml. Parse and validate appbay.yaml with Zod schemas. Errors are recorded but do not block other apps.
Upstream transform – For apps with an upstream.source, apply namespace isolation first (internal network creation, volume prefixing, shared network aliases). This runs before variable resolution so that scope references inside the upstream compose are visible to the resolver.
Resolve variables – Evaluate ${{scope.KEY}} references against the variable store named by the scope prefix. Only project has a populated store ($APPBAY_HOME/etc/system.yaml’s domain:); see the warning under Variable resolution. Magic generators (${password:N}, ${uuid}, etc.) are evaluated and persisted.
Select overlays – Evaluate when clauses against the active app set; merge matching fragments into the compose model.
Apply traits – Transform the compose model (add Traefik config, GPU devices, auth middleware, etc.) in declaration order.
Render – Write final compose YAML to var/lib/renders/<app>/
Plan/Diff – Compare rendered output against the previous render on disk; produce a redacted diff.

After compilation, docker compose up -d is invoked with the rendered artifacts. The compile phase is deterministic: the same inputs always produce the same rendered output.

title: Managing Apps
text:
Appbay discovers apps by scanning $APPBAY_HOME/etc/apps/. Each subdirectory containing a docker-compose.yml is an app. The directory name is the app name – no registration step required.
$APPBAY_HOME/etc/apps/
  ollama/
    docker-compose.yml        # required
    appbay.yaml               # optional
    .env                      # optional, compose convention
  jellyfin/
    docker-compose.yml
    appbay.yaml
  nextcloud/
    docker-compose.yml
    appbay.yaml
The layout is flat. There is no forced nesting by project, environment, or collection. Organizational grouping is handled by metadata in appbay.yaml, not by directory hierarchy.


To add a new app, create a directory and place your docker-compose.yml inside:
mkdir -p ~/.appbay/etc/apps/myapp
cat > ~/.appbay/etc/apps/myapp/docker-compose.yml << 'EOF'
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
EOF
The app is immediately discoverable:
appbay list
# NAME           PROJECT   ENVIRONMENT  APPBAY.YAML  COMPOSE FILE
# myapp          default   default      no           docker-compose.yml
# whoami         default   default      no           docker-compose.yml
No appbay.yaml is needed for simple apps. It is only required when Compose alone cannot express what you need – traits, upstream transforms, overlays, or scope assignments.

title: Managing Apps
text:
The appbay.yaml file
appbay.yaml is an optional metadata file with three clearly separated sections: scope, upstream/overrides/overlays (the application model), and traits.
Here is a complete example:
# ---- Scope: where does this app belong? ----
namespace: homelab.prod
collection: [ai-stack, gpu-apps]
operator: local
shared_network: [appbay_shared]
tags:
  tier: compute
  team: ml

# ---- Application model: what does the compose look like? ----
upstream:
  source: ./docker-compose.upstream.yml
  expose:
    - web
  services:
    exclude:
      - debug-tools

overrides:
  web:
    environment:
      - CUSTOM_HEADER=X-Appbay

overlays:
  - when: [ollama]
    services:
      web:
        environment:
          - OLLAMA_URL=http://ollama_web:11434

# ---- Traits: declarative transformations ----
traits:
  - type: backup
    schedule: "0 2 * * *"
    retention: 7

services:
  web:
    traits:
      - type: ingress
        host: myapp.${{project.DOMAIN}}
        port: 3000
        exposure: external
        tls:
          staging: false
      - type: gpu
        variant: nvidia

Scope section
The scope section assigns organizational metadata:









Key
Cardinality
Default
Description




project
single
default
Variable scope namespace (${{project.KEY}} resolution)


environment
single
default
Deployment variant (variable values, certs)


collection
multi
[]
Operational grouping for batch operations

single
local
Which operator runs this app


shared_network
multi
[appbay_shared]
Shared networks for cross-app communication

key-value

Arbitrary metadata for filtering and UI grouping





Application model section
The application model section controls how Compose files are processed:
upstream.source – Points to a stock upstream compose file. Appbay ingests it with zero edits required. Use this when you pull a docker-compose.yml directly from a project’s repository and want to keep it unmodified.
upstream.expose – Lists which services are aliased onto the shared network. Internal services remain on the app’s private network and are not accessible to other apps.
upstream.services.exclude – Filters out services you do not need (e.g., development tools, test runners).
overrides – Static compose overrides keyed by original service name. Merged on top of the upstream compose.
overlays – Conditional fragments applied when peer apps are active. See Conditional Overlays.


Traits section
Traits are declared at two levels:

App-level traits in the top-level traits: array apply to the entire app (e.g., backup, auth, scoped-env).
Service-level traits in services.<name>.traits apply to a specific service (e.g., ingress, gpu, hooks).

title: Managing Apps
text:
Upstream compose ingestion
One of Appbay’s key features is accepting stock upstream compose files with zero modifications. Many open-source projects ship a docker-compose.yml that you can use directly.

How it works

Place the upstream file in your app directory (e.g., as docker-compose.upstream.yml).
Reference it in appbay.yaml:

upstream:
  source: ./docker-compose.upstream.yml
  expose:
    - web

Appbay creates an internal network per app to preserve upstream service discovery. Services that reference each other by name (e.g., app connecting to db) continue to work because the internal network is maintained.
Only services listed in upstream.expose are aliased onto the shared network. This provides namespace isolation – two apps can both have a service named db without conflicts.



Namespace isolation
When Appbay compiles an app, it applies namespace isolation:

Container names are prefixed: appbay.<app>.<service>
Volume names are prefixed: <app>_<volume>
An internal network is created per app for service-to-service communication (<app>_internal)
Exposed services are aliased onto the shared network with the format <app>_<service> (underscore)

This means you can run multiple apps that have identically named services (like web, db, redis) without any port or name collisions.


Example: ingesting Nextcloud
# apps/nextcloud/appbay.yaml
namespace: homelab.prod
collection: [productivity]

upstream:
  source: ./docker-compose.upstream.yml
  expose:
    - app
  services:
    exclude:
      - cron    # not needed, using hooks instead

overrides:
  app:
    environment:
      - NEXTCLOUD_TRUSTED_DOMAINS=${{project.DOMAIN}}

services:
  app:
    traits:
      - type: ingress
        host: cloud.${{project.DOMAIN}}
        port: 80
        exposure: external
        tls:
          staging: false
The upstream docker-compose.upstream.yml stays completely unmodified. Appbay applies overrides, traits, and namespace isolation during compilation.

title: Managing Apps
text:
App selection
Appbay provides several ways to select which apps to operate on:

By name
appbay up ollama webui tts       # deploy specific apps
appbay down jellyfin             # stop one app
appbay restart nextcloud         # restart one app


By collection
appbay up --collection ai-stack  # all apps in the ai-stack collection


All apps
appbay up --all                  # deploy everything
appbay ps --all                  # status of all apps


Presets
Save a named selection of apps for reuse:
# Save a preset
appbay presets save my-stack --apps "ollama,webui,whisper" --description "AI and media apps"

# List presets
appbay presets list

# Load a preset (prints app names; pipe to appbay up)
appbay presets load my-stack

# Delete a preset
appbay presets delete my-stack
Presets are stored as YAML files in $APPBAY_HOME/etc/presets/.


Service selection within an app
App selection determines which apps are deployed. Service selection within an app uses standard Docker Compose profiles. Pass --profile directly to docker compose after compiling with Appbay:
appbay compile ollama
docker compose --profile debug -f ~/.appbay/var/lib/renders/ollama/docker-compose.yml up -d
Appbay does not reinvent service-level selection – Compose profiles work as normal on the rendered output.

text:
Deleting an app
To remove an app and optionally its volumes:
# Stop and remove containers, keep volumes (--force required to confirm)
appbay delete myapp --force --keep-volumes

# Stop and remove everything including volumes
appbay delete myapp --force
--force is always required to confirm the deletion. Without it, the command exits with an error. --keep-volumes controls whether Docker volumes are preserved.

title: Traits
text:
Traits are declarative transformations that add capabilities to your apps. Instead of manually editing Compose files to add Traefik labels, GPU device mappings, or auth middleware, you declare what you want in appbay.yaml and the compiler generates the correct configuration.
Traits follow OAM (Open Application Model) rules:

Applied in the order they are declared
One configuration per trait type per service
Some traits declare conflictsWith to prevent incompatible combinations

Traits are scoped to either the service level (applied to a specific Compose service) or the app level (applied to the entire app).

title: Traits
text:
Ingress trait
Scope: service
The ingress trait generates reverse-proxy routing configuration for a service, as a file the proxy picks up — not as Docker labels.
Which proxy it emits for is an installation-level setting, not a trait property (see Ingress providers below). By default it emits Traefik dynamic config; set ingress_provider: caddy and the same trait emits a Caddy site block instead. The trait’s properties are identical either way.

Basic example
# apps/nextcloud/appbay.yaml
services:
  nextcloud:
    traits:
      - type: ingress
        host: cloud.homelab.example.com
        port: 80
        exposure: external
        tls:
          staging: false
Service-scoped traits like ingress are declared under services.<name>.traits to target a specific service. Service-scoped traits must always be declared at the service level – they cannot be moved to the top-level traits: array (which is reserved for app-scoped traits like auth and backup).


Properties









Property
Type
Default
Description




host
string
required
The hostname for routing (supports ${{project.DOMAIN}})


port
number
required
Target port on the service


exposure
enum
both
internal (LAN only), external (WAN), or both


tls
object
omit for no TLS
TLS config: { staging: false } for prod, { staging: true } for LE staging


service
string
(the service it is declared under)
Target compose service. Required when the trait is declared at app level in a multi-service app; inherited automatically when declared under a service.





Exposure modes
Traefik runs with two entrypoints:

websecure (port 443) — for HTTPS traffic
web (port 80) — HTTP (used for both exposure as a plain HTTP fallback)

The exposure property controls which entrypoints the router listens on:
# LAN-only service
- type: ingress
  host: nas.home.lan
  port: 80
  exposure: internal

# Internet-facing service with TLS
- type: ingress
  host: blog.example.com
  port: 3000
  exposure: external
  tls:
    staging: false

# Available on both LAN and WAN (HTTP + HTTPS)
- type: ingress
  host: cloud.example.com
  port: 80
  exposure: both
  tls:
    staging: false


TLS certificates
When tls is set, the ingress trait configures Let’s Encrypt certificate resolution via the Traefik certResolver mechanism. Use staging: true while testing to avoid Let’s Encrypt rate limits; switch to staging: false for production:
# Production certificate
tls:
  staging: false

# Staging certificate (untrusted, for testing)
tls:
  staging: true


Using scoped variables
services:
  jellyfin:
    traits:
      - type: ingress
        host: jellyfin.${{project.DOMAIN}}
        port: 8096
        exposure: external
        tls:
          staging: false
The ${{project.DOMAIN}} reference resolves at compile time from the domain: line in $APPBAY_HOME/etc/system.yaml.
⚠️ It is the only scope reference that resolves, and DOMAIN is the only key. The other settings in etc/system.yaml (home:, project:, container_runtime:) are not variables. ${{environment.KEY}} and ${{service.KEY}} are accepted by the parser but nothing populates those maps, so they always fail — see Scope Model. For a per-deployment value, use a plain Compose ${VAR} read from the app’s .env.


Ingress providers








provider
emits
where




traefik (default)
dynamic config YAML for the file provider
etc/apps/traefik/config/dynamic/<app>.yml


caddy
a Caddy site block
etc/apps/caddy/config/dynamic/<app>.caddy



Choose it once per installation:
appbay init --ingress-provider caddy






NoteWhy this is not a trait property



Every app on a host is fronted by the same proxy. If each app declared its own, two apps could disagree about which proxy is deployed — and the loser would emit a perfectly valid config file for a proxy that is not running. No error, no route, nothing to grep for.


Both providers compose the same way. The ingress trait owns the routing; the auth trait contributes the authentication layer from its own file, and the proxy assembles them:

Traefik composes by name — auth defines a middleware, the router references it.
Caddy composes by file glob — the site block carries import auth/<app>-*.caddy, and auth drops that file beside it. An app with no auth trait produces no fragment, the glob matches nothing, and the configuration is still valid.

So adding or removing the auth trait never requires touching the ingress trait, under either provider.






Warning



Under Caddy, exactly one emitter may open a site block — two files declaring the same host is an ambiguous site definition error. That owner is the ingress trait, because it knows the host, the upstream service and the port. Anything the auth trait contributes is a bare directive list imported into that block, never a site block of its own.

title: Traits
text:
GPU trait
Scope: service
The GPU trait adds GPU device passthrough to a service. It auto-detects the appropriate configuration from operator-reported runtime facts.

Basic example
# apps/ollama/appbay.yaml
services:
  web:
    traits:
      - type: gpu
With no variant specified, the operator detects the available GPU and selects the right configuration automatically.


Properties









Property
Type
Default
Description




variant
enum
auto-detect
nvidia (Docker GPU runtime), cdi (Container Device Interface), or rocm (AMD ROCm)


count
number
1
Number of GPUs to allocate. Use -1 for all GPUs


devices
string[]
omit
CDI device names (e.g., ["all"]). Only used with variant: cdi


service
string
(the service it is declared under)
Target compose service. Required when the trait is declared at app level in a multi-service app; inherited automatically when declared under a service.





GPU variants
The compiler generates different Compose configurations based on the selected variant:
nvidia (Docker GPU runtime):
services:
  web:
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: 1
              capabilities: [gpu]
cdi (Container Device Interface):
services:
  web:
    devices:
      - nvidia.com/gpu=all
rocm (AMD GPU):
services:
  web:
    devices:
      - /dev/kfd
      - /dev/dri
    group_add:
      - video
      - render


Auto-detection
When variant is omitted (the default), the compiler probes the host and selects the variant based on what is available:

If CDI is supported → cdi
If an NVIDIA GPU is present → nvidia
If an AMD GPU is present → rocm

If no GPU is detected and no explicit variant is set, the deploy fails with an error.


Do I need to install anything for GPU support?
Probably not. Run this one command:
docker run --rm --device nvidia.com/gpu=all ubuntu:24.04 nvidia-smi -L
If it lists your GPU, Appbay will use it and you have nothing to install — no nvidia-container-toolkit, no nvidia-container-runtime. Your host already has a CDI spec (usually /etc/cdi/nvidia.yaml), and Docker 25+ and Podman 4.1+ read those directly.
If the command fails, you need one of:

a CDI spec — generate one with nvidia-ctk cdi generate --output=/etc/cdi/nvidia.yaml, which you can run from a container rather than installing the toolkit; or
the NVIDIA container runtime, which is the older path Appbay’s nvidia variant uses.

Appbay picks CDI when a spec is present, because it needs nothing else on the host.

title: Traits
text:
Auth trait
Scope: app
The auth trait protects an app behind the Caddy Security edge — a browser login portal plus role-based authorization. It requires the Caddy ingress provider (appbay init --ingress-provider caddy); Traefik remains a supported ingress mode but is not an authentication provider.

Basic example
# apps/nextcloud/appbay.yaml
traits:
  - type: auth
    enabled: true


Properties









Property
Type
Default
Description




mode
enum
portal
Auth mode (portal)


policy
enum
authenticated
Access policy (authenticated or deny)


group
string
omit
Optional identity role required in addition to the built-in admin role


enabled
boolean
true
Toggle auth on/off per app


service
string
(the service it is declared under)
Target compose service. Required when the trait is declared at app level in a multi-service app; inherited automatically when declared under a service.





How it works

During compilation, the auth trait generates a Caddy Security authentication route in etc/apps/caddy/config/dynamic/auth/<app>-security.caddy and an authorization policy in etc/apps/caddy/config/security/policies/<app>.caddy.
The ingress trait’s site block imports the auth fragment, so the app’s host is protected by the Caddy Security portal.
Requests to the app are authenticated by the Caddy Security portal and authorized by the generated policy. On success, Caddy injects Remote-User, Remote-Email, and Remote-Groups headers that the app reads to identify the user.



Restricting to a group
group: names an identity role the user must hold. Roles are namespaced authp/<name>, and you may write either form — group: admins and group: authp/admins are equivalent.
traits:
  - type: auth
    policy: authenticated
    group: admins          # only members of authp/admins may reach this app
The generated policy allows the built-in admin role plus the group you named:
allow roles authp/admin authp/admins
A user who authenticates successfully but holds neither role receives 403 Forbidden. Create a user who does hold it with:
appbay edge users create alice --email alice@example.com --roles admins --generate --reveal






ImportantRestart the edge after changing a policy



Authorization policies are imported inside Caddy’s global block, and --watch does not reload those — per-app routes and auth fragments hot-reload, policies do not.
appbay down caddy && appbay up caddy
Skipping this makes a policy change appear to have no effect, which looks exactly like broken role matching and is not.








NoteEdge users sign in to AppBay too



The people who sign in to your deployed apps are edge users, managed with appbay edge users — and since RFC-001 §1 they are also the accounts that sign in to AppBay itself, which is a stack behind the same edge. Reaching the control plane additionally requires the authp/admin role. The vault’s master password stays a separate credential. See Credentials.




Verifying it actually restricts
⚠️ A successful login by a member proves nothing. A member is admitted whether the policy matches or falls through to something permissive. The only test that distinguishes an enforcing policy from an inert one is a user who authenticates and should be refused:
scripts/journeys/s25-edge-authz.sh    # asserts member reaches the app AND outsider is 403


Per-app toggle
Auth can be enabled globally and disabled for specific apps:
# apps/public-site/appbay.yaml
traits:
  - type: auth
    enabled: false    # this app does not require login

title: Traits
text:
Hooks trait
Scope: service
The hooks trait adds auxiliary containers and configuration using three Compose-native patterns. Appbay never rewrites entrypoints.

Properties









Property
Type
Default
Description




pattern
enum
required
init, sidecar, or config


image
string
busybox:latest
Container image (init and sidecar patterns)


command
string
omit
Command to run (single string, not array)


volumes
string[]
omit
Volume names to mount (init and sidecar patterns)


content
string
omit
Inline file content (config pattern only)


share
object
omit
Namespace sharing: { network: bool, pid: bool, ipc: bool }


service
string
(the service it is declared under)
Target compose service. Required when the trait is declared at app level in a multi-service app; inherited automatically when declared under a service.





Init pattern
A one-shot container that must complete before the target service starts:
services:
  app:
    traits:
      - type: hooks
        pattern: init
        image: busybox:latest
        command: "mkdir -p /data/subdir && chown -R 1000:1000 /data"
        volumes:
          - app-data
This generates a Compose service with depends_on using condition: service_completed_successfully. The init container gets restart: no.


Sidecar pattern
A long-running companion service that runs alongside the main service:
services:
  app:
    traits:
      - type: hooks
        pattern: sidecar
        image: prom/node-exporter
        volumes:
          - metrics-data
The sidecar gets restart: unless-stopped and shares volumes with the target service.

Namespace sharing
Sidecars can share Linux namespaces with the target container using the share block:
services:
  app:
    traits:
      - type: hooks
        pattern: sidecar
        image: nicolaka/netshoot
        command: "tcpdump -i any -w /captures/app.pcap"
        share:
          network: true
          pid: true
        volumes:
          - captures-data








Share flag
Docker effect
Use case




network
network_mode: service:<target>
localhost access to target ports, packet capture


pid
pid: service:<target>
Process inspection, signal delivery


ipc
ipc: service:<target>
Shared memory (rare)



Port forfeiture rule: When share.network is true, the sidecar cannot publish its own ports (Docker limitation). Any ports: declaration is automatically stripped.
Auto-dependency: When any share flag is set, depends_on: { <target>: { condition: service_started } } is added automatically.



Config pattern
Injects a configuration file using Compose configs with inline content (requires Compose v2.23.1+):
services:
  app:
    traits:
      - type: hooks
        pattern: config
        content: |
          {
            "debug": false
          }
The config is mounted into the target service at a generated path (/<app>-<service>-hook-config). No additional containers are created.

title: Traits
Traits
text:
Secrets trait
Scope: service
The secrets trait declares URI-based secret references that are resolved at deploy time. See Secrets Management for the full documentation.
⚠️ Since RFC-001 §3.2 a manifest may carry only vault:// references — the storage backend is an installation choice, and a manifest naming one breaks on any host that chose differently.
traits:
  - type: secrets
    refs:
      DB_PASSWORD: vault://nextcloud/DB_PASSWORD
      SMTP_KEY: vault://nextcloud/SMTP_KEY
      API_TOKEN: vault://nextcloud/API_TOKEN
      ENCRYPTION_KEY: vault://nextcloud/ENCRYPTION_KEY

Injection modes

runtime-env (default): Secrets are injected as process environment variables to docker compose. They never touch disk.
wrapper (opt-in): Secrets are mounted as tmpfs files via the wrapper hook pattern.

title: Traits
text:
Backup trait
Scope: app
The backup trait configures scheduled backups for an app’s data:
traits:
  - type: backup
    schedule: "0 2 * * *"       # daily at 2 AM
    retention: 7                 # keep 7 days
    volumes:
      - data                     # which volumes to back up
      - config

Properties









Property
Type
Default
Description




schedule
cron string
required
Backup schedule in cron format


retention
number
7
Number of days/copies to retain


volumes
string[]
all
Which volumes to include (defaults to all app volumes)





System backup
In addition to per-app backup, Appbay supports system-level backup that covers:

Appbay configuration files (etc/)
State store (var/lib/state/)
Secrets metadata (URIs only, never values)
SQLite database

System backup is configured globally, not per-app.

title: Traits
text:
Trait conflicts
Some traits are incompatible with each other. Trait definitions declare conflictsWith to prevent invalid combinations. The compiler reports a validation error if conflicting traits are applied to the same service.
Example: if a hypothetical static-ip trait conflicts with ingress, applying both to the same service would produce:
ERROR: Trait conflict on service "web" in app "myapp":
  "static-ip" conflicts with "ingress"
  Remove one of the conflicting traits.

title: Traits
text:
Trait declaration order
Traits are applied in the order they are declared. This matters when traits modify the same parts of the Compose model. Each trait’s transform() receives the Compose state as left by all previous traits.
services:
  web:
    traits:
      - type: ingress      # runs first: creates Traefik router config
        host: app.example.com
        port: 3000
      - type: gpu          # runs second: adds GPU devices to services.web
        variant: nvidia

title: User Guide
text:
Appbay is a Docker-native PaaS control plane that treats Docker Compose as the application model. Rather than replacing Compose or inventing a new orchestration layer, Appbay augments your existing Compose files with traits, scoped variables, conditional overlays, secrets management, and namespace isolation – all while keeping standard docker compose as the runtime contract.
You can eject any app at any time and run it with plain docker compose up. Appbay adds structure; it never locks you in.

title: User Guide
text:
Who is Appbay for?
Appbay serves three overlapping use cases:

Homelab

You host upstream applications (Jellyfin, Nextcloud, Vaultwarden) with minimal friction. You want ingress routing, TLS certificates, and forward authentication without hand-editing Traefik labels for every app.

Applab

You run curated application stacks for a team or department. You need consistent environments, secret management, and the ability to deploy a named collection of apps with one command.

Devlab

You build applications that require extensive configuration, iteration, and environment-specific wiring. You need scoped variables, conditional cross-app wiring, and deterministic renders so that the same inputs always produce the same outputs.

title: User Guide
text:
What you will learn
This guide walks through every aspect of using Appbay:

Getting Started – Install Appbay, deploy your first app, and verify it works.
Core Concepts – Understand apps, traits, overlays, scopes, collections, and operators.
Managing Apps – Directory conventions, appbay.yaml, upstream ingestion, and app selection.
Traits – The seven built-in traits: ingress, gpu, auth, hooks, scoped-env, secrets, and backup.
Conditional Overlays – Declarative cross-app wiring with when clauses.
Secrets Management – URI-based secret references, auto-generation, and verification.
CLI Reference – All commands with examples and flags.
Web UI – Dashboard, deploy flow, logs, shell, and settings.

title: User Guide
text:
Design principles
Before diving in, these principles shape every feature in Appbay:

Filesystem is the source of truth. Your appbay.yaml and docker-compose.yml files on disk are authoritative. SQLite is a metadata cache that can be rebuilt at any time with appbay rebuild-cache.
Deterministic renders. Same inputs always produce the same outputs. Generated values are stored once and reused.
Secrets never leak. No plaintext secrets appear in logs, rendered artifacts, plan diffs, or events.
CLI works without the web frontend. Validate, compile, deploy, and eject all work with no server container running.
Standard Compose output. Everything Appbay produces is runnable with docker compose directly.

title: Appbay
text:
Appbay manages Docker Compose apps — ingress, TLS, authentication, secrets and namespacing — without taking your Compose files away from you.
You can eject any app at any time and run it with plain docker compose up. Appbay adds structure; it never locks you in.

title: Appbay
text:
Try it
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kundeng/appbay-cli/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
appbay setup --domain home.lan
That installs a single binary — no Node.js, no Bun, nothing else on the host — then walks you through creating the install, its secret vault, and the reverse proxy.
Getting Started →

title: Appbay
text:
What you get







Your Compose files stay yours
Upstream files are never modified. Appbay layers policy on top and renders a new file.


Traits instead of label soup
type: ingress gives an app a hostname, TLS and forward-auth, rather than a dozen hand-written proxy labels.


Secrets that never reach disk in the clear
An encrypted local vault, with five injection modes depending on how the app expects to read them.


One API, two interfaces
The CLI and the web UI call the same code, so they cannot disagree about what your system is doing.


Docker or Podman
Choose the runtime once, at init. Rootful Podman on RHEL-family hosts is supported and tested, SELinux included.

title: Appbay
text:
Where to go next

Getting Started — install, deploy an app, reach it in a browser.
Core Concepts — apps, traits, overlays, scopes and collections.
Traits — the full list, with what each one emits.
Deployment — running Appbay itself, on a server or in a container.
Reference — every CLI command, every schema field.







NoteAlpha



Appbay is alpha. The runtimes verified end-to-end are Docker and rootful Podman; rootless Podman runs apps but cannot own the edge’s ports. See Getting Started for the specifics, including the RHEL-family notes.

title: App Catalog
text:
The catalog is a collection of pre-configured app definitions — each one a docker-compose.yml paired with an appbay.yaml that wires the right traits (ingress, secrets, backup, auth) with sensible defaults.
Instead of writing appbay.yaml from scratch for every app, browse the catalog, install what you need, and customize.

title: App Catalog
text:
Browse the catalog
# List all available apps
appbay catalog list

# Filter by category
appbay catalog list --category monitoring

# Filter by readiness level
appbay catalog list --readiness augmented

# Search by name, tag, or description
appbay catalog search ai

# JSON output for scripting
appbay catalog list --json
Example output:
NAME         READINESS  CATEGORY    SOURCE   DESCRIPTION
--------------------------------------------------------
grafana      augmented  monitoring  bundled  Observability dashboards with Prometheus metrics
it-tools     raw        utilities   bundled  Collection of handy developer utilities
n8n          augmented  automation  bundled  Workflow automation tool with 400+ integrations

title: App Catalog
text:
Install an app
# Install with defaults
appbay install uptime-kuma

# Provide required values non-interactively
appbay install n8n --set N8N_DB_PASSWORD=mypass --set N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=mykey

# Overwrite an existing installation
appbay install open-webui --force

# Skip post-install validation
appbay install it-tools --no-validate

The catalog entry is copied to $APPBAY_HOME/etc/apps/<name>/
If the app has required inputs, you’re prompted (or use --set)
A .env file is written with your values + defaults
appbay validate runs to verify the result

After install, the app is ready to deploy:
appbay up n8n

title: App Catalog
text:
Readiness levels
Each catalog entry declares how much Appbay integration it has:








Level
What you get
What you may need to do




raw
Upstream compose only
Provide env vars, configure traits yourself


augmented
Compose + curated appbay.yaml with traits
Fill in required inputs (domain, passwords)


native
Compose + appbay.yaml written together
Nothing — works out of the box



Most catalog entries are augmented — someone has already configured ingress, secrets, backup, and other traits with good defaults.

title: App Catalog
text:
Catalog sources
The catalog supports multiple sources:

Bundled — ships with Appbay (cloned at appbay init)
External — git repos you add yourself

# Add an external catalog source (future)
appbay catalog add-source community https://github.com/example/appbay-catalog

# Update catalog sources
appbay catalog update

title: App Catalog
text:
Required inputs
Some apps need values before they can deploy — a domain name, database password, or API key. These are declared in the catalog entry’s catalog.yaml as required_inputs:
required_inputs:
  - name: N8N_DB_PASSWORD
    description: PostgreSQL password
    type: secret
    auto_generate: true
  - name: N8N_HOST
    description: Public domain for n8n
    type: string
    default: "n8n.${{project.DOMAIN}}"

type: secret with auto_generate: true — a password is generated automatically if you don’t provide one
type: string with default — pre-filled, you can accept or override
Scoped variables like ${{project.DOMAIN}} are resolved from your project.yaml

title: App Catalog
text:
Post-install customization
After install, you own the files. Customize freely:
# Edit the appbay.yaml directly
vi ~/.appbay/etc/apps/n8n/appbay.yaml

# Or use the config CLI
appbay config n8n set traits.0.exposure external

# Or use the web UI's traits panel and config editor
appbay server start
# Navigate to http://localhost:3000 → Apps → n8n → Config

title: App Catalog
text:
Catalog entry structure
Each catalog entry is a directory:
n8n/
  catalog.yaml          # Browse metadata (description, tags, required inputs)
  appbay.yaml           # Deployment config (traits, scope, upstream ref)
  docker-compose.yml    # Upstream compose file
  .env.defaults         # Optional: default environment values
catalog.yaml is for browsing and install logic. appbay.yaml is the deployment config that ends up in your apps directory.

title: Web UI
text:
Dashboard


The Appbay web UI is a Next.js application that provides a visual management interface for your Docker apps. It communicates with the backend via tRPC (type-safe API calls) and Server-Sent Events (real-time logs and status updates).
The web UI is optional – the CLI and compiler work without it. The web UI adds real-time dashboards, visual diffs, log streaming, a built-in shell, and a deploy planner.


appbay server start

On first visit, Appbay enters “setup mode” because no admin account exists yet. You will see a “Create Admin Account” form. Enter a username and password to create the admin account. All subsequent visits require login.

APPBAY_DEV_AUTH=true appbay server start

Dashboard

The dashboard is your home screen. It provides an at-a-glance view of your entire Appbay installation.

What you see

System health – Docker status, Compose version, disk space, GPU availability
App overview – Total apps, running count, stopped count, apps with issues
Running apps – Cards showing each running app with its services, ports, and uptime
Recent deployments – The last several deploy operations with status (success, failed, in progress)

App cards

App name and namespace
Running/stopped status indicator

title: Web UI
text:
App Detail
Route: /apps/:name
The app detail screen shows everything about a specific app.

Panels
Services panel – Lists all Compose services in the app with their container status, ports, image, and resource usage.
Traits panel – Shows all attached traits with their configuration. Service-level traits are grouped under their service. Conflict warnings are displayed if applicable.
Overlays panel – Shows all conditional overlays with their when clause and activation status. Active overlays are highlighted in green; inactive ones are grayed out. Activation is evaluated against the installed app set — the same question the compiler asks — so the panel and the rendered output always agree.

View logs (jumps to the log viewer)
Open the app URL in a new tab
Edit configuration
Trigger a recompile and deploy

title: Web UI
text:
Deploy Flow
Route: /deploy
The deploy screen provides a guided workflow: compile, review diff, confirm, and apply.

Step 1: Select apps
Choose which apps to deploy by:

Clicking individual app checkboxes
Selecting a collection
Using “Select All”



Step 2: Compile
Click “Compile” to run the compiler pipeline. Appbay resolves traits, overlays, scoped variables, and secrets, then generates rendered Compose files.


Step 3: Review diff
The deploy screen shows a redacted diff comparing the rendered output against the currently deployed state. Secret values are always shown as [REDACTED].
  services:
    web:
      environment:
+       OLLAMA_BASE_URL: http://ollama_web:11434
        DB_PASSWORD: [REDACTED]
      image: ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:latest
You can expand each app’s diff to see the full changes.


Step 4: Confirm and apply
Click “Apply” to deploy. The screen switches to a live progress view showing:

Current deployment phase (pulling, creating, starting)
Real-time log output (streamed via SSE)
Per-app status indicators (pending, in progress, success, failed)



Deploy history
Route: /deployments

Route: /deployments/:id

Secrets Screen
Route: /secrets
The secrets screen has three tabs controlled by a segmented toggle:

References tab
Global view of all secret URI references across all apps. Provider status strip at the top shows resolution health per provider (vault, keepass, file, env, sops). Searchable and filterable by provider.

text:
Auth Screen
Route: /auth
Application access and authentication. Application routes and access policies are declared in each app’s appbay.yaml manifest and compiled into the selected edge configuration. Caddy installations use the integrated Caddy Security login portal; manage its local identities with appbay edge users. Traefik remains ingress-only.

title: Web UI
text:
Doctor Screen
Route: /doctor
The doctor screen runs the same checks as appbay doctor and displays results visually.

Authentication
The web UI does not authenticate anyone. The Caddy Security edge does, before a request reaches it at all, and injects the identity as a Remote-User header.







Access path
Requirement




All web pages
the edge’s identity header


tRPC API calls
the same header, read in createContext


SSE connections
the same header, checked on connect


health.get endpoint
none — so bootstrap can check a server nobody has signed into

Through the edge portal, which owns the session. AppBay has none to end.

Route: /identity — the same EdgeIdentityStore the CLI drives, so the two never disagree.

text:
Before installing Appbay, make sure you have the following on your system:








Requirement
Minimum version
Check command




Docker or Podman
Docker 24.0+ / Podman 4.9+
docker --version / podman --version


Compose v2
v2.23.1+
docker compose version / podman compose version


SELinux (RHEL-family only)
Permissive or Disabled
getenforce



Compose v2.23.1 or later is required because Appbay uses the configs resource with inline content, which was introduced in that release.


On RHEL-family hosts (Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, Alma), AppBay requires SELinux to be Permissive or Disabled. This is a prerequisite, not a recommendation — an Enforcing host can start the control plane and serve the UI, and then fail every deploy made from it.
getenforce                       # must print Permissive or Disabled
sudo setenforce 0                # until the next reboot
To make it durable, set SELINUX=permissive in /etc/selinux/config and reboot.
The cause is not something a relabel can fix. The control-plane container reaches the container runtime through a unix socket, and the denial is SELinux’s unix_stream_socket connectto check against the API service’s own process label. Measured on Fedora 43 with rootful podman 5.6.2:








SELinux mode
Socket label
Result




Enforcing
var_run_t
permission denied


Enforcing
container_file_t (relabelled with :z)
permission denied — a relabel is not enough


Permissive
either
works



A per-container escape hatch also exists if you cannot change the host mode — see the RHEL-family notes below for control_plane_selinux: unconfined, which disables confinement for the control-plane container only rather than for the host.






NoteWhy AppBay does not ship an SELinux policy module



A policy module granting just connectto would keep confinement, and was considered. It is not planned: it means shipping, versioning and supporting a compiled policy per distribution for a control plane that is already the most privileged container AppBay runs. Requiring Permissive is the honest trade, and stating it up front beats an install that looks healthy and cannot deploy.





Appbay drives whichever container binary you configure. Point it at Podman once, at init:
appbay init --container-runtime podman
That writes container_runtime: podman to $APPBAY_HOME/etc/system.yaml, and every command Appbay issues from then on invokes podman. It also works on re-init, so a configuration management run can converge it repeatedly — the command reports created, updated or unchanged so you can drive changed-state from a read-back rather than an exit code.






ImportantThis chooses a binary, not a daemon



If you have installed the Docker CLI pointed at a rootful podman.socket via DOCKER_HOST, leave the runtime as docker — that is Podman’s own documented arrangement, and the binary you want invoked really is docker. Set podman only when you want the podman binary itself run.








ImportantRHEL-family hosts: three things that stop AppBay before it starts



All three were found by running AppBay on Fedora with SELinux enforcing, and none of them reproduces on Ubuntu — Docker simply does not have these behaviours.
1. SELinux blocks bind mounts unless they are labelled. A container process runs as container_t and cannot read a file labelled user_home_t, which is what everything under your home directory is. The failure is a bare permission error with no mention of SELinux:
Error: reading config from file: open /etc/caddy/Caddyfile: permission denied
The edge crash-looped 62 times on exactly this, while the deploy reported “configuration rejected” — sending the operator to inspect a config file that was perfectly valid.
AppBay now adds the :z (shared relabel) option to every bind mount it generates, so its own apps are fine. If you write your own compose with a bind mount, add it yourself:
volumes:
  - ./config:/etc/app/config:ro,z     # the ,z is not optional on SELinux hosts
Docker accepts and ignores the option, so it is safe to write unconditionally.
2. Image names must be fully qualified. RHEL-family hosts set short-name-mode = "enforcing" in /etc/containers/registries.conf, so Podman refuses to guess a registry — and in any automation there is no TTY to prompt on:
Error: short-name resolution enforced but cannot prompt without a TTY
Use the full path. Note that Docker Hub official images live under library/:
image: docker.io/library/postgres:16     # official image
image: docker.io/grafana/grafana:latest  # user image
Docker assumes docker.io silently, which is why an unqualified name works there and fails here.
3. The control plane container cannot reach the runtime socket, even as root. This one only bites if you run the web UI via appbay server start; the CLI on the host is unaffected. Measured on Fedora 43 with rootful Podman:
$ sudo podman exec appbay.server docker version
permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API at unix:///var/run/docker.sock
The server starts, reports healthy and serves the UI — and then every deploy from the web fails. Relabelling the socket does not fix it: the denial is SELinux’s unix_stream_socket connectto check against the API service’s own process label, which no file label can satisfy.
The switch is one line in $APPBAY_HOME/etc/system.yaml:
control_plane_selinux: unconfined
Then appbay server start again. Confirm with sudo podman exec appbay.server docker version, which should print your Podman version.
⚠️ Understand what you are turning off. This adds security_opt: [label=disable] to the control-plane container — the most privileged container AppBay runs. It is off by default and absent means off, so nothing changes until you set it. The alternative that keeps confinement is an SELinux policy module granting just connectto; AppBay does not ship one yet.








NoteRootless Podman: supported for experimentation, not for the edge



AppBay’s alpha runtime matrix is Docker and rootful Podman. Rootless Podman is not gated on, and these are the specific reasons — all measured on Fedora 43, not inferred:
It cannot bind the edge’s ports. net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start is 1024 on a stock host, so a rootless container cannot take :80 or :443:
podman run --rm -d -p 80:80 busybox sleep 20   →  refused
The ingress edge exists to own those ports, so a rootless install has no edge. Apps themselves run fine.
Rootless and rootful are separate worlds, and AppBay does not model which one you are in. They keep different stores:
rootless   /run/user/1000/containers
rootful    /run/containers/storage
A rootless podman ps sees none of the rootful containers and vice versa. In practice this means appbay init run as your user creates appbay_shared in the rootless store, and a later sudo appbay up cannot see it:
Error: External network [appbay_shared] does not exists
appbay doctor is honest here — run under sudo it correctly reports the network missing rather than reading the other context’s state. But nothing records which context an install is bound to, and nothing warns when you switch. Pick one and stay in it. If you use rootful (recommended, and required for the edge), run every appbay command with the same privilege, including init.
This is a known limitation with an open design decision behind it; it is not a bug you need to report.








Warningcompose version succeeding does not mean compose works



Podman hands compose off to an external provider (docker-compose if installed, podman-compose otherwise). A provider much newer than the Podman it talks to can report its version perfectly and then fail to create containers — measured with podman 6.0.2 and docker-compose v5.1.2, which fails up with no such image on an image Podman demonstrably holds.
Verify by deploying something, not by reading a version banner:
appbay doctor          # necessary, not sufficient
appbay up <some-app>   # this is the actual test
AppBay enforces a floor of podman-compose 1.5.0. Older releases cannot parse the long-form env_file AppBay emits (Compose Spec v2.24+) and fail with:
TypeError: join() argument must be str, bytes, or os.PathLike object, not 'dict'
Measured: podman-compose 1.0.6 creates containers perfectly from a hand-written compose file and still cannot run AppBay — which is why the floor is set from AppBay’s own output, not from whether the provider starts.
If the pairing fails, select the other provider — it is configuration, not a rebuild:
export PODMAN_COMPOSE_PROVIDER=podman-compose
# or set it permanently in containers.conf(5):  [engine] compose_providers








Note



Appbay ships as a single compiled binary — no Node.js, Bun, or other runtime is needed on the target machine.








Tip



Looking for the full bootstrap journey? See bootstrap.md for the complete single-binary path — doctor → init-system → init → setup → first app — with exact commands, expected output, and failure modes for both human and AI operators.

title: Getting Started
text:
Installation

One-line install (recommended)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kundeng/appbay-cli/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
The installer detects your OS and architecture (Linux/macOS, x64/arm64), downloads the latest release binary, and places it in /usr/local/bin/appbay (if writable) or ~/.local/bin/appbay. Override with APPBAY_INSTALL_DIR.


Self-update
Once installed, update to the latest release with:
appbay update


Build from source (for contributors)
If you want to develop on Appbay itself, clone and build:
# Requires: Node.js 22+, pnpm, Bun
git clone https://github.com/kundeng/appbay-cli.git
cd appbay-cli
pnpm install
pnpm turbo build
The CLI binary is built at ./apps/cli/dist/appbay. You can symlink it into your PATH:
ln -s "$(pwd)/apps/cli/dist/appbay" ~/.local/bin/appbay


Verify installation
appbay version

title: Getting Started
text:
Set up Appbay
The setup command is the recommended way to get started. It handles everything: scaffolding directories, creating the Docker network, configuring the Caddy Security edge (ingress + authentication), and deploying system apps:
appbay setup
The wizard prompts for your project name and base domain, then runs through 7 steps automatically. At the end, it prints bootstrap credentials for the admin user.

Non-interactive mode
For scripting or CI, pass all options as flags:
appbay setup --domain homelab.example.com --project homelab --yes
Authentication is a property of the edge you choose, not a flag. There are two supported edges and a host runs exactly one, because both bind ports 80 and 443:
# Ingress + browser login + role-based authorization (default)
appbay setup --domain homelab.local --ingress-provider caddy --yes

# Ingress only — TLS and routing, no authentication
appbay setup --domain homelab.local --ingress-provider traefik --yes






WarningThe auth trait requires the Caddy Security edge



On a Traefik installation an app declaring type: auth fails to compile with a message saying so. Traefik is a supported ingress mode; it is not an authentication provider.








Tip



macOS users: Appbay works with OrbStack (recommended) and Docker Desktop. No special configuration needed – appbay setup detects your Docker runtime automatically.




Check setup status
After setup (or if you’re debugging a partial install), run:
appbay setup --status
This shows which steps are complete and which are missing.


Low-level alternative: appbay init
If you only need the directory scaffold without deploying system apps:
appbay init --project homelab --domain homelab.example.com --yes
This creates the $APPBAY_HOME structure but does not configure the edge or deploy anything.

title: Getting Started
text:
Check prerequisites
Run doctor to verify that all dependencies are installed and configured correctly:
appbay doctor
The doctor runs seventeen checks: platform detection; the container runtime and whether the current user can reach it without sudo; Compose presence and version; APPBAY_HOME; the shared network and whether names actually resolve on it; healthcheck start_period; Traefik and Caddy Security config; vault status; KeePass database and keepassxc-cli; server status; GPU availability; and SOPS.
Checks are required or optional, and the distinction matters when reading the output: an optional check that fails is a warning, not a failure. A missing GPU does not make the install unhealthy.
Everything is named after the runtime you configured, so on a Podman install it reports Podman and podman-compose — it will not tell you to install Docker. The web UI’s Doctor screen runs this same code, so the two cannot disagree.

title: Getting Started
text:
Deploy your first app
Appbay ships with a whoami starter app – a lightweight HTTP service that returns request headers. Deploy it:
appbay up whoami
Behind the scenes, Appbay:

Discovers the app in $APPBAY_HOME/etc/apps/whoami/
Reads docker-compose.yml (and appbay.yaml if present)
Resolves traits, overlays, and scoped variables
Renders the final compose file to var/lib/renders/
Runs docker compose up -d with the rendered output


Verify it works
curl http://localhost:8888
You should see the container’s hostname and request headers printed back.


Check app status
appbay ps whoami
APP       SERVICE   STATUS    PORTS
whoami    web       running   0.0.0.0:8888->80/tcp


View logs
appbay logs whoami --follow
Press Ctrl+C to stop following.


Stop the app
appbay down whoami

title: Getting Started
text:
Start the web UI
The web UI provides a dashboard, deploy planner, log viewer, config editor, and built-in shell. Start the control plane:
appbay server start
server start writes the edge’s route to the control plane and binds port 3000 to loopback in the same step, so the way in is https://appbay.<your-domain> — the same Caddy Security portal that guards your apps.
Sign in with the edge administrator appbay setup printed. There is no second account and no first-run setup screen.






ImportantIt is the account appbay setup printed



This used to be a different credential: a control-plane administrator in $APPBAY_HOME/etc/control-plane/users.yaml, created on a first-run screen, deliberately never synchronised with the edge. RFC-001 §1 removed it — the UI is a stack behind the edge like any other, so the edge account is the account.
⚠️ It must hold the authp/admin role. The control plane’s route carries an admin-only policy, narrower than an app’s default, because it is the one stack that can reach the container runtime socket.
⚠️ Without an edge route the server does not fall back to a password. It has no way to authenticate anyone and says so instead of serving. If you see that, set domain: in etc/system.yaml and re-run appbay server start.





Appbay Dashboard


Once you sign in, the dashboard shows your running apps grouped by collection, system health, and the overlay relationship graph.

title: Getting Started
text:
Next steps
You now have a working Appbay installation. From here:

Read Core Concepts to understand how apps, traits, and overlays work together.
Read Managing Apps to learn how to add your own applications.
Run appbay list --all to see all available apps, including system apps.
Try appbay up --collection ai-stack to deploy an entire collection at once (after adding apps to that collection).

title: Getting Started
text:
Troubleshooting

appbay init fails with permission errors
Make sure you have write access to the target directory. By default, this is ~/.appbay. You can override it with --dir or by setting the APPBAY_HOME environment variable.


Docker socket not accessible
Appbay needs access to the Docker socket. If you get “permission denied” errors:

Linux: Add your user to the docker group: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER (log out and back in)
macOS (OrbStack): OrbStack handles socket permissions automatically. Make sure OrbStack is running.
macOS (Docker Desktop): Ensure Docker Desktop is started and the socket path is accessible.



Compose version too old
Appbay requires Docker Compose v2.23.1 or later. Update with:
# If using Docker Desktop, update Docker Desktop
# If using standalone compose plugin:
docker compose version  # check current
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install docker-compose-plugin

title: CLI Reference
text:
The Appbay CLI is a single compiled binary built with Bun. It operates offline — it imports packages/core directly and calls Docker via docker compose shell invocations. There is no tRPC client; the CLI does not connect to the running Appbay server for app management commands.
appbay <command> [args...] [flags]

title: CLI Reference
text:
Bootstrap commands

appbay init
Scaffold the $APPBAY_HOME directory, create project structure, and seed system app definitions.
appbay init
appbay init --project homelab --domain homelab.example.com
appbay init --dir /opt/appbay



Flag
Description




--project <name>
Name of the default project


--domain <name>
Base domain for ingress routing


--dir <path>
Path for $APPBAY_HOME (default: ~/.appbay)


--yes
Non-interactive: accept all defaults without prompting



This command is idempotent – running it again does not overwrite existing configuration.


appbay doctor
Check prerequisites, runtime health, and system readiness.

NoteThe vault password is one of three



It unlocks vault.enc and nothing else. The password you use to sign in to AppBay, and the passwords your users use to sign in to deployed apps, are separate and independently recovered — see The Three Credentials.

title: Secrets Management
text:
Overview
Appbay uses URI-based references for secrets. Instead of embedding secret values in configuration files, you reference them by URI. Secrets are resolved at deploy time and injected into the runtime environment – never written to rendered artifacts in plaintext.
This design ensures that:

Secrets are never committed to version control
Secrets are never visible in plan diffs or logs
Secrets can be rotated by updating the source, not by editing app configs
Different environments can use different secrets via the same URI patterns

title: Secrets Management
text:
URI schemes
Appbay v1 supports six URI schemes for secret references:

vault:// (default — local vault)
The local vault (AES-256-GCM encrypted KeePass .kdbx file) is Appbay’s default secrets provider. Secrets are auto-generated if missing and stored locally.
traits:
  - type: secrets
    refs:
      DB_PASSWORD: vault://prod/nextcloud/db-password
      SMTP_KEY: vault://prod/shared/smtp-api-key
      REDIS_PASS: vault://nextcloud/REDIS_PASSWORD
The URI format is vault://<path>/<KEY>: the last segment is the key, and everything before it is the path. The path may be any depth — vault://a/b/c/d/FIELD is valid and resolves FIELD under a/b/c/d.
In practice every shipped manifest uses two segments, scoped by app: all 66 vault:// references across both catalogs are vault://<app>/<KEY>, e.g. vault://photoprism/PHOTOPRISM_DB_PASSWORD. There is no environment segment — that was a documentation artefact, not a shape the parser has ever required.
The local vault provides:

Auto-generation of missing secrets (magic vars: ${password:32}, ${uuid}, etc.)
KeePass-compatible .kdbx format (viewable in KeeWeb or KeePassXC)
No external dependencies — runs entirely on the local filesystem



file:// (file-based secrets)
⚠️ Not permitted in appbay.yaml since RFC-001 §3.2. The provider still exists and still resolves, but a manifest may only carry vault:// references — the storage backend is an installation choice, and a manifest naming one breaks on any host that made a different choice. The example below is kept to document the URI form.
References a file on the host filesystem. The file should contain only the secret value with no trailing newline. Files should be permissions-restricted (0400 or 0600).
# check-docs-manifests: ignore
traits:
  - type: secrets
    refs:
      TLS_CERT: file:///etc/ssl/certs/homelab.pem
      TLS_KEY: file:///etc/ssl/private/homelab.key
      SSH_KEY: file:///home/appbay/.ssh/deploy_key
This is the simplest approach and requires no external service.


env:// (environment variables)
⚠️ Not permitted in appbay.yaml since RFC-001 §3.2. The provider still exists and still resolves, but a manifest may only carry vault:// references — the storage backend is an installation choice, and a manifest naming one breaks on any host that made a different choice. The example below is kept to document the URI form.
References an environment variable on the host where Appbay runs. Useful for secrets provided by CI/CD pipelines or system-level configuration.
# check-docs-manifests: ignore
traits:
  - type: secrets
    refs:
      GITHUB_TOKEN: env://GITHUB_TOKEN
      CLOUDFLARE_API_KEY: env://CF_API_KEY
The host environment variable must be set when appbay up runs. If it is not set, the deploy fails with an actionable error.


vault:// (local encrypted vault)
The built-in local vault. Zero external dependencies — an AES-256-GCM encrypted JSON file at $APPBAY_HOME/var/lib/vault.enc. Secrets are scoped by app name.
traits:
  - type: secrets
    provider: vault
    refs:
      DB_PASSWORD: vault://kestra/DB_PASSWORD
      API_KEY: vault://kestra/API_KEY
The URI format is: vault://<scope>/<key> where scope is typically the app name. Flat vault://KEY uses scope “default” (shared across apps).
Auto-generation: If a vault secret doesn’t exist on first deploy, it’s auto-generated (32-char hex by default). Add ?gen=password:24 for a different format. Subsequent deploys reuse the stored value.
# Initialize the vault (auto-generates master password)
appbay secrets init

# Manually set a secret
appbay secrets set kestra/DB_PASSWORD mypassword

# Import secrets from an app's .env file
appbay secrets import kestra

# List vault contents
appbay secrets vault


keepass:// (KeePass database)
⚠️ Not permitted in appbay.yaml since RFC-001 §3.2. The provider still exists and still resolves, but a manifest may only carry vault:// references — the storage backend is an installation choice, and a manifest naming one breaks on any host that made a different choice. The example below documents the URI form only.
References a value inside a KeePass .kdbx file via keepassxc-cli. Useful when you already manage secrets in KeePass.
# check-docs-manifests: ignore
traits:
  - type: secrets
    provider: keepass
    refs:
      DB_PASSWORD: keepass:///path/to/vault.kdbx#group/entry/Password


sops:// (encrypted files)
⚠️ Not permitted in appbay.yaml since RFC-001 §3.2. The provider still exists and still resolves, but a manifest may only carry vault:// references — the storage backend is an installation choice, and a manifest naming one breaks on any host that made a different choice. The example below documents the URI form only.
References a value inside a SOPS-encrypted file. The file is decrypted at deploy time using the host’s SOPS configuration (age, GPG, or cloud KMS).
# check-docs-manifests: ignore
traits:
  - type: secrets
    refs:
      DB_PASSWORD: sops://secrets.enc.yaml#database.password
      API_KEY: sops://secrets.enc.yaml#services.api.key
The URI format is: sops://<file-path>#<yaml-path>
SOPS-encrypted files can be safely committed to version control since they contain only encrypted values.

title: Secrets Management
text:
Declaring secrets
Secrets are declared using the secrets trait in appbay.yaml. Because the secrets trait is service-scoped, it must be declared under services.<name>.traits:
# apps/nextcloud/appbay.yaml
services:
  nextcloud:
    traits:
      - type: secrets
        refs:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: vault://prod/nextcloud/db-password
          NEXTCLOUD_ADMIN_PASSWORD: vault://prod/nextcloud/admin-password
          SMTP_PASSWORD: vault://nextcloud/SMTP_PASSWORD
          REDIS_PASSWORD: ${password:24}
Each key in refs becomes an environment variable injected into the service at runtime.

title: Secrets Management
text:
Auto-generation
Magic generators in refs values are evaluated once at compile time and their output is stored in the state store. Subsequent compiles reuse the stored value for deterministic output. This works with ${password:N}, ${uuid}, ${base64:N}, and ${hash}.
services:
  nextcloud:
    traits:
      - type: secrets
        refs:
          # Generates a strong 32-char password on first compile; reuses the same value after that
          REDIS_PASSWORD: ${password:32}
          INSTALL_ID: ${uuid}
For KeePass-backed secrets, auto-generation is handled by the KeePass database — create entries before the first deploy using KeeWeb or KeePassXC.

title: Secrets Management
text:
Injection modes
Secrets can be injected in two ways:

Runtime-env (default)
Secrets are resolved and passed as process environment variables to docker compose up. They exist only in the container’s runtime environment and are never written to disk.
services:
  app:
    traits:
      - type: secrets
        injection: runtime-env    # this is the default
        refs:
          DB_PASSWORD: vault://myapp/DB_PASSWORD


Wrapper-file (file-based, no env exposure)
For applications that read secrets from files (Docker-secrets-aware apps, Java apps reading /run/secrets/), the wrapper-file mode writes secrets to a shared Docker volume as files. No environment variable exposure.
services:
  app:
    traits:
      - type: secrets
        injection: wrapper-file
        refs:
          DB_PASSWORD: vault://myapp/DB_PASSWORD
          API_KEY: vault://myapp/API_KEY
At deploy time:

A one-shot shepherd container writes resolved values as files to a Docker volume
The target service mounts the volume read-only at /run/secrets/<app>/
Each secret becomes a file: /run/secrets/myapp/DB_PASSWORD, /run/secrets/myapp/API_KEY

No env exposure: docker inspect shows zero secret environment variables — secrets exist only as files in the volume.


Entrypoint-wrapper (opt-in, highest security)
For apps that read process.env at startup, the entrypoint-wrapper mode rewrites the container’s entrypoint to run the small appbay-inject binary, which decrypts a per-app secret bundle from a mounted volume and then execs the original process. Secrets are set as shell variables via export — they inherit into the process but are not visible to docker inspect.
services:
  app:
    traits:
      - type: secrets
        injection: entrypoint-wrapper
        refs:
          DB_PASSWORD: vault://myapp/DB_PASSWORD
Trade-off: The compose file is rewritten (entrypoint + command + configs), and the container gains a dependency on the injector binary and its volume. No Appbay service needs to be running — the bundle is on disk. This is the highest-security option but breaks the “upstream compose unchanged” guarantee.

title: Secrets Management
text:
Security guarantees
Appbay enforces the following security rules for secrets:

Never in plaintext
Secret values never appear in:

Rendered compose files – URIs are resolved at runtime, not during compilation
Plan diffs – secret changes show [REDACTED] instead of values
Logs – both CLI and web UI redact any string matching a known secret pattern
SQLite cache – only secret URIs (not values) are stored in secrets_meta
Git diffs – since secrets are not in config files, they cannot be committed
SSE events – deployment status messages redact secret values



Example: redacted plan diff
  services:
    web:
      environment:
-       DB_PASSWORD: [REDACTED]
+       DB_PASSWORD: [REDACTED]
        DB_HOST: postgres-db
Even when a secret changes, the diff only shows that it changed, not what it changed to.

title: Secrets Management
text:
Scoped secrets
Secrets can differ per deployment by varying the vault path.
⚠️ The environment.yaml mechanism this section used to describe does not exist. It told you to define an ENV var in etc/projects/<name>/environments/<env>.yaml and interpolate it into the URI. Nothing reads that file — ProjectConfigSchema and EnvironmentConfigSchema have no non-test consumers, and the string "projects" is never joined into a path — so ${{environment.ENV}} resolves to nothing and the URI never substitutes.
Until a value store exists, scope secrets by writing the path you want directly, or by distinguishing them at the app level:
services:
  nextcloud:
    traits:
      - type: secrets
        refs:
          DB_PASSWORD: vault://nextcloud/DB_PASSWORD
The path is any depth you like, so a deployment that genuinely needs separate values can carry the distinction in the path itself — vault://prod/nextcloud/DB_PASSWORD and vault://dev/nextcloud/DB_PASSWORD are both valid and resolve independently. What does not work is interpolating a scope reference into the URI, because no store populates one.

title: Secrets Management
text:
Secret lifecycle
Vault secrets are authoritative for initial provisioning. Understanding when secrets are read by containers is critical for safe rotation.

Stateful services (databases)
Database containers (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis with persistence) only read password environment variables on first initialization — when the data volume is empty. After that, the password is stored inside the database’s own data directory. Changing the vault secret after initialization has no effect on the running database.
To rotate a database password after first deploy:

appbay secrets set myapp/DB_PASSWORD newpassword — updates the vault
Connect to the database container and run the appropriate command:

Postgres: ALTER USER myuser PASSWORD 'newpassword';
MySQL: ALTER USER 'myuser'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'newpassword';
MongoDB: db.changeUserPassword("myuser", "newpassword")

appbay up myapp — restarts the app container with the new env var



Stateless services (apps, APIs)
Application containers that read secrets from environment variables on every startup will pick up vault changes on restart. appbay up triggers a container recreation, which re-reads the environment.
Examples: API keys, JWT signing secrets, SMTP credentials, OAuth client secrets.


Rotation summary








Secret type
Vault change + redeploy sufficient?
Additional action needed?




App API keys

No

Yes (existing sessions invalidated)

title: Secrets Management
text:
Best practices
Use the local vault for production. The file:// and env:// schemes are convenient for development, but the local vault provides encrypted storage, auto-generation, and KeePass-compatible management.
Run appbay secrets check before deploying. Make it part of your workflow to catch missing or misconfigured secrets before they cause deploy failures.
Use auto-generation for database passwords. Let Appbay generate strong passwords for internal services like databases and Redis. You never need to type or remember these.
Keep SOPS files in version control. Since they are encrypted, they are safe to commit. This gives you versioned, auditable secret storage without an external service.
Avoid env:// for long-lived secrets. Environment variables are visible to any process on the host. Use file:// with restricted permissions (0400) or the local vault for sensitive credentials.

title: The Three Credentials
text:
AppBay has three passwords. They are deliberately independent, they are never synchronized with each other, and each is recovered by a different command.
Mixing them up is the most common way to lock yourself out of something while holding a password that works perfectly well for something else.

title: The Three Credentials
text:
The two domains










What it opens
Where it lives
Recover with




Edge user
The apps you deployed — and the AppBay UI
the edge’s identity store
appbay edge users reset-password


Master password
vault.enc, your encrypted secrets
var/lib/secrets/master-password
appbay secrets vault rotate-password








flowchart TD
  A[operator] -->|signs in to AppBay| E[Edge user]
  U[your users] -->|sign in to deployed apps| E
  A -->|unlocks secrets| V[Master password]

  E --> EF[edge identity store]
  V --> VF[vault.enc]












NoteThere used to be three



A separate control-plane account opened the AppBay UI, stored in etc/control-plane/users.yaml and reset with appbay admin reset-password. RFC-001 §1 removed it: the UI is a stack behind the edge like Portainer or Open WebUI, so it authenticates the same way they do. One store, one place to revoke someone.
Its edge route carries an admin-only policy (authp/admin), narrower than an app’s default, because the control plane is the one stack that can reach the container runtime socket. So “can open Grafana” still does not mean “can reconfigure the installation” — that distinction moved from a separate password to a role.








ImportantWhy the remaining two stay separate



Signing in is not the same as decrypting. Someone who can reach the UI should not thereby hold the key to every secret in the vault, and the vault must stay openable by the CLI on a host where no edge is running at all. AppBay never syncs them.

title: The Three Credentials
text:
Which one do I want?
“I can’t log in to the AppBay UI.”
That is an edge user, same as any app. RFC-001 §1 removed AppBay’s separate control-plane account: the web UI sits behind the Caddy Security edge like Portainer or Open WebUI, so there is no second password and no etc/control-plane/users.yaml.
appbay edge users reset-password alice --generate --reveal
⚠️ Only members of authp/admin can reach the control plane — its edge route carries an admin-only policy, narrower than an app’s default, because it is the one stack that can reach the container runtime socket.
If the UI says it is not reachable through the edge, that is a deployment problem rather than a login one: the server refuses to serve when nothing has authenticated the request. Run appbay init --ingress-provider caddy, set domain: in etc/system.yaml, then appbay server start.
“An app asks me to sign in and my password doesn’t work.”
That is an edge user — a person who signs in to a deployed app, not to AppBay.
appbay edge users list
appbay edge users reset-password alice --generate --reveal
“A deploy failed saying a secret could not be resolved.”
That is the vault password.
appbay secrets vault rotate-password






WarningA lost vault password is unrecoverable



vault.enc is encrypted with it. Rotation re-encrypts using the current password, so it requires the current one. There is no reset — losing it means losing the stored values, though the references to them in your manifests remain intact.

title: The Three Credentials
text:
Reading a password prompt correctly
Every command that takes a password accepts three forms, and the difference matters:
# From a pipe — the value never appears in argv
printf %s "$SECRET" | appbay edge users reset-password alice --password-stdin

# Generated and shown exactly once
appbay edge users reset-password alice --generate --reveal

# Generated and NOT shown (for automation that will set it elsewhere)
appbay edge users reset-password alice --generate






NoteWhy --password-stdin exists



Passing a secret as a command argument puts it in /proc/<pid>/cmdline, where every local user can read it for the life of the process. Fine for a throwaway value in your own shell; not fine for a configuration-management run seeding real credentials on a shared host.

title: The Three Credentials

What survives what








Event

Vault

TipDeleting the cache is safe



appbay.db holds job history and a query mirror — all disposable. Since RFC-001 §1 it holds no credentials and no sessions at all: identity comes from the edge on every request, so deleting the database does not even log anyone out.

title: The Three Credentials
text:
Retired commands
appbay authelia, appbay auth and appbay admin are gone. Running any of them prints what replaced it and exits non-zero, so a script that still calls them fails rather than appearing to succeed.

title: Native Installation
text:
Native mode builds and runs the CLI directly from a checkout rather than installing a released binary. Use this when you are:

Developing Appbay itself – iterating on the compiler, traits, or CLI commands.
Debugging – you want a binary built from your working tree.
Contributing – you are preparing a pull request and need the full toolchain.

The web control plane is a separate component distributed as a container image; it is not built from this repository, so there is no server to run natively. appbay server start runs it as a container whichever way you installed the CLI.
For production or homelab use, prefer the Compose deployment.

The web control plane is a separate component distributed as a container image; it is not built from this repository, so there is no server to run natively. appbay server start runs it as a container whichever way you installed the CLI.
