text: A production deployment builds on the Compose deployment with additional hardening: a reverse proxy with TLS, system app infrastructure, authentication enforcement, and a backup strategy. This page covers each layer.

title: Production Deployment
text:
System app deployment order
Appbay ships infrastructure system apps that must be deployed in dependency order. Deploy them in this sequence – each depends on the previous:

caddy – Integrated ingress, TLS termination, and the Caddy Security edge (authentication + authorization). Protects apps that enable the auth trait.

# Deploy the edge:
appbay up caddy
Traefik remains a supported ingress-only mode (appbay init --ingress-provider traefik), but authentication requires the Caddy Security edge.
Each system app is a standard Appbay app with its own appbay.yaml and docker-compose.yml in $APPBAY_HOME/etc/apps/. The definitions are seeded during appbay init.

title: Production Deployment
text:
Reverse proxy setup
Appbay generates Traefik dynamic configuration as YAML files (file provider), not Docker labels. When you assign the ingress trait to a service, the compiler writes a routing file to var/lib/renders/<app>/traefik/dynamic/<app>.yml.

Traefik configuration
The system Traefik app is pre-configured with:

HTTP entrypoint on port 80 (redirects to HTTPS)
HTTPS entrypoint on port 443
File provider watching $APPBAY_HOME/var/lib/renders/*/traefik/dynamic/
Let’s Encrypt ACME resolver for automatic TLS certificates

Example ingress trait on a service:
# apps/jellyfin/appbay.yaml
services:
  jellyfin:
    traits:
      - type: ingress
        host: "media.${{project.DOMAIN}}"
        port: 8096
        exposure: both
        tls:
          staging: false    # Set true to use Let's Encrypt staging
This generates a Traefik dynamic config file with the router, service, and middleware definitions for the jellyfin service.

title: Production Deployment
text:
TLS certificates
How certificates are issued depends on which edge you selected at appbay setup. The two providers are mutually exclusive — one host, one owner of ports 80 and 443.

Traefik
Uses Let’s Encrypt for automatic issuance.
Staging certificates – Set tls.staging: true in the ingress trait during initial setup to avoid rate limits while testing. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers but verify that ACME challenges work.
Production certificates – Set tls.staging: false (the default) for valid certificates. Ensure your DNS records point to the host and ports 80/443 are reachable from the internet.
Certificate storage is handled by Traefik’s built-in ACME store, persisted in a volume.


Caddy
Caddy issues from Let’s Encrypt automatically with no configuration. For names a public CA cannot validate, it falls back to its own internal issuer — a locally-trusted CA it manages itself. On a .test.local host the served certificate reports:
issuer=CN = Caddy Local Authority - ECC Intermediate
This is why config/tls/ ships empty: the site blocks import /etc/caddy/tls/*.caddy as a zero-match glob, so an install using the internal issuer needs no file and no placeholder. Browsers will warn unless you trust Caddy’s local root.

Institutional ACME (InCommon and similar)
Institutional CAs require external account binding: your ACME account is tied to credentials the institution issues you. Copy the shipped example to enable it:
cd "$APPBAY_HOME/etc/apps/caddy/config/global"
cp acme.caddy.example acme.caddy
The file contains placeholders only; the values are read from process environment at deploy time:
email {$ACME_EMAIL}
acme_ca {$ACME_CA}

acme_eab {
    key_id {$ACME_EAB_KID}
    mac_key {$ACME_EAB_HMAC}
}






ImportantThree ways this fails quietly



acme_eab takes a block, not two inline arguments. Written as acme_eab {$ACME_EAB_KID} {$ACME_EAB_HMAC} the whole config is rejected and the edge will not start — which takes every deployed app down with it, since the edge is the only path to them. AppBay shipped that form and fixed it; if you copied an older example, use the block above.
Do not wrap the file in { }. It is imported inside the base global options block, so it holds option directives only. An outer block is a syntax error.
Do not add a global acme_dns block here. It is silently ignored: the config loads without complaint and certificates simply never issue by DNS. DNS-01 belongs in a site block or a tls directive, and needs an image built with the DNS provider compiled in (xcaddy build --with github.com/caddy-dns/cloudflare).


Never write the secrets into acme.caddy. docker compose config prints file contents in cleartext; AppBay injects process environment precisely so the values need not be on disk. Store them in the vault (appbay secrets set) and reference them as vault:// URIs.


Validating before you rely on it
An EAB misconfiguration fails at account registration, not renewal, so it reads like a network problem rather than a configuration one. Check the config parses and the directives actually reach Caddy’s adapted output before pointing a real domain at it:
VM=<host> ./scripts/journeys/s25-acme-config-validate.sh
That proves everything up to the CA round-trip. The round-trip itself needs your real credentials and a publicly resolvable domain.

title: Production Deployment
text:
Security hardening

The control plane has no password of its own
RFC-001 §1 removed AppBay’s own accounts. The UI sits behind the Caddy Security edge and the person signing in is whoever the edge identifies, so there is no first-run admin and no separate password to harden. Harden the edge account instead:
appbay edge users reset-password alice --generate --reveal
⚠️ Only members of authp/admin reach the control plane — its route carries an admin-only policy, narrower than an app’s default, because it is the one stack that can reach the container runtime socket. Grant that role deliberately.
⚠️ appbay server start binds port 3000 to loopback whenever it wrote an edge route, so the edge is the only way in. Do not set APPBAY_BIND=0.0.0.0 in production: with the port reachable, the identity header the UI trusts can be set by anyone who can reach it.


Disable dev auth
Never run production with APPBAY_DEV_AUTH=true. This flag bypasses all authentication and is intended only for local development. The Compose deployment does not set this flag by default.


Docker socket access
The server container mounts the Docker socket read-only (/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro) and uses the docker CLI directly via spawnSync for container operations.


Network isolation

appbay_shared – Apps that need to communicate join this network. Each app also gets its own <app>_internal network for service-to-service discovery within the app.

title: Production Deployment
text:
Backups

What to back up
Back up the entire $APPBAY_HOME directory. The critical subdirectories are:








Path
Contents
Regenerable?




etc/apps/
App definitions (appbay.yaml, docker-compose.yml)
No – these are your source of truth


etc/projects/
Project and environment configs
No


var/lib/state/
Generated values, active app set
No – generated values are random


var/lib/renders/
Rendered compose output
Yes – appbay compile regenerates


appbay-data named volume
SQLite metadata cache (compose deployments)
Yes – appbay rebuild-cache regenerates


var/log/
Log files
Not critical





Backup strategy
# Simple tarball backup
tar czf appbay-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz $APPBAY_HOME/etc $APPBAY_HOME/var/lib/state

# Restore
tar xzf appbay-backup-20260503.tar.gz -C /
appbay rebuild-cache    # Regenerate SQLite from restored files
appbay compile          # Regenerate renders


App data backup
App data (Docker volumes) is separate from Appbay configuration. Use the backup trait to schedule volume snapshots:
# appbay.yaml
traits:
  - type: backup
    schedule: "0 2 * * *"    # Daily at 2 AM
    retention: 7             # Keep 7 days
    volumes:
      - nextcloud_data
      - nextcloud_db

title: API Endpoint Reference
text: All API endpoints are tRPC procedures served at /api/trpc/. Except where noted, all procedures require an authenticated caller — which since RFC-001 §1 means the Caddy Security edge has authenticated the person and injected Remote-User. There is no session cookie and no bearer token; AppBay neither issues nor reads one.

title: API Endpoint Reference
text:
Notation

query – read-only, idempotent
mutation – writes data or triggers side effects
Input types shown in Zod notation. z.string() means a string, z.object({...}) means an object with the listed fields.

title: API Endpoint Reference
text:
auth
Who the Caddy Security edge says you are, and whether this server is behind one at all. Both procedures are public — they have to be, since they are what the UI calls to find out whether anybody is authenticated.
⚠️ AppBay has no accounts of its own since RFC-001 §1. There is no login, no signup and no first-run setup here; identity is resolved from the edge’s Remote-User header on every request. See Credentials.

auth.me
Return the identity the edge asserted, or null. Safe to call without one — no error is thrown.

Type: query
Input: none
Output: { user: { id: string, username: string } | null }
Auth: none



auth.edgeAuth
Whether this server is behind the Caddy Security edge at all.

Type: query
Input: none
Output: { enabled: boolean }
Auth: none

Not a permission check — it lets the UI tell two very different “no user” states apart. Enabled with no user means the edge is there but injected no identity, so its authorization policy is wrong; disabled means the server is not behind an edge, cannot authenticate anyone, and is refusing to serve.






Note





auth.setupRequired and auth.rotateSession were removed
RFC-001 §1 deleted AppBay’s own accounts, so there is no first-run setup to report and no control-plane session to rotate. Identity is resolved from the edge on every request.

text:

title: API Endpoint Reference
text:
edge
Protected router. Edge identities are the accounts the Caddy Security portal accepts — for your deployed apps, and since RFC-001 §1 for the AppBay control plane too, which is a stack behind the same edge.
It has a CLI counterpart (appbay edge users), and that is not a second authentication configuration path: both drive the same EdgeIdentityStore in @appbay/core. One store, one hasher, one reload — the interfaces differ only in how input is collected.
⚠️ Reaching the control plane additionally requires the authp/admin role. Its edge route carries an admin-only policy, narrower than an app’s default, because it is the one stack that can reach the container runtime socket.

edge.listUsers
List local edge identities. An empty list is a normal state on a fresh install, not an error.

Type: query
Input: none
Output: { users: [{ id, username, email, roles[], created, lastModified }] }







Warning



Password hashes are never returned. Only the fields above cross the API boundary.




edge.createUser
Create an edge identity with a generated password.

Type: mutation
Input: { username, email, roles?: string[] } (roles default to ["user"])
Output: { user, password, edgeRestarted }

Roles given without an organization are namespaced to authp/, which is what app access policies match on. The password is returned once and only once — only a bcrypt hash is stored, so it cannot be retrieved again.


edge.resetPassword
Reset an edge identity’s password to a newly generated one. Every previous credential is revoked, so the old password stops authenticating immediately.

Type: mutation
Input: { username }
Output: { user, password, edgeRestarted }

text:
catalog
Protected router. Browse and install curated catalog entries.

catalog.list
List catalog entries, optionally filtered.

Type: query
Input: { source?, readiness?, category?, query? } (all optional)
Output: { entries: [{ ...entry, source, hasAppbayYaml, hasCompose }], errors: [{ dir, message }] }

errors reports entries that could not be read. It is part of the normal response, not an exception — one malformed entry must not hide the rest of the catalog.


catalog.get
Fetch a single catalog entry by name.

Type: query
Input: { name }
Output: the entry, with its source and file presence flags



catalog.search
Search catalog entries.

Type: query
Input: { query }
Output: matching entries



catalog.install
Install a catalog entry into this AppBay home.

Type: mutation
Input: { name, values?: Record<string,string>, force? }
Output: the install result from catalogInstall()

text:
deployments

deployments.applyPlan
Apply a pre-compiled rendered compose file synchronously. The client sends the YAML string produced by plans.compile; the server writes it to disk and runs docker compose up -d. HTTP response is held open until the compose command completes.

Type: mutation
Input: { appName: string, rendered: string }
Output: { success: boolean, deployId: string }



deployments.enqueue
Async deploy path preferred by the web UI. Writes the rendered compose file to disk and enqueues a "deploy" job. Returns immediately — callers poll jobs.get(jobId) for status and subscribe to SSE deploy.status / deploy.logs for real-time progress.

Type: mutation
Input: { appName: string, rendered: string }
Output: { jobId: string, deployId: string }



deployments.up
Compile and deploy apps in one step.

Type: mutation
Input: { apps: string[] }
Output: { success: boolean, errors: string[] }



deployments.down
Stop running apps.

Type: mutation
Input: { apps: string[], volumes?: boolean } (volumes defaults to false)
Output: { success: boolean, errors: string[] }



deployments.restart
Restart running apps (down then up for each).

Type: mutation
Input: { apps: string[] }
Output: { success: boolean, errors: string[] }



deployments.fullDeploy
Run the whole compile → write → deploy pipeline for a selection of apps, emitting deploy.status events over SSE as it goes. This is what the Deploy screen drives; the narrower procedures above act on already-rendered output.

Type: mutation
Input: { apps?: string[], collection?: string } — omit both to deploy everything
Output: the deploy result, including per-app status and a deployId correlating the emitted events



deployments.list
List deployment history.

Type: query
Input: { limit?: number } (optional, defaults to 50)
Output: Deploy[] with { id, appName, status, startedAt, completedAt }



deployments.get
Get details for a specific deployment.

configs

configs.list
List saved config presets.

Type: query
Input: none
Output: ConfigPreset[]



configs.save
Save a named app selection preset. Creates or overwrites the preset file in $APPBAY_HOME/etc/configs/.

Type: mutation
Input: { name: string, description?: string, apps: string[] } (apps is a list of app names to save)

Load a config preset by name. Returns null if not found.

Input: { name: string }
Output: void







NotePresets and per-app configuration are two different things in one router



Everything above operates on saved presets (named app selections in $APPBAY_HOME/etc/configs/). Everything below operates on one app’s own configuration — its appbay.yaml values and its .env variables. They share a router and nothing else.




configs.getAppConfig
Read an app’s whole appbay.yaml configuration.

Type: query
Input: { appName: string }
Output: { found: boolean, config: object | null, path: string | null }



configs.getAppConfigValue
Read a single configuration value from an app’s appbay.yaml.

Type: query

Output: the resolved value

secrets.check

secrets.vault

Type: query

title: API Endpoint Reference
text:
jobs
Read-only access to the in-process job queue backed by SQLite. All Docker-heavy operations (deploy, pull-images, eject, rebuild-cache) run as jobs so the HTTP response is not held open. Clients poll jobs.get or subscribe to SSE deploy.status / deploy.logs for progress.

jobs.get
Get a single job by ID. Returns null if the ID does not exist. Suitable for 1–2 second polling while a job is running.

Type: query
Input: { id: string }
Output: { id, type, status, payload, createdAt, startedAt?, completedAt?, error? } | null



jobs.list
List recent jobs, most-recent first.

Type: query
Input: { type?: "deploy" | "backup" | "rebuild-cache" | "pull-images" | "eject", limit?: number } (all optional, limit defaults to 50)
Output: { id, type, status, createdAt, startedAt?, completedAt?, error? }[]



jobs.cancel
Cancel a pending job. Running jobs cannot be cancelled.

Type: mutation
Input: { id: string }
Output: { cancelled: boolean }



jobs.rebuildCache
Enqueue a rebuild-cache job. Re-scans $APPBAY_HOME/etc/apps/ and regenerates the SQLite cache. Safe to run at any time; does not affect running containers.

Type: mutation
Input: none
Output: { success: boolean, jobId: string | null }



jobs.pullImages
Enqueue a pull-images job. Pulls the latest Docker images for all system apps (Caddy, Traefik, etc.). Never touches running containers.

Type: mutation
Input: none
Output: { success: boolean, jobId: string | null }



jobs.ejectAll
Enqueue an eject job. Compiles all user apps and writes rendered compose YAML to $APPBAY_HOME/eject/<app-name>/docker-compose.yml. Never modifies running containers.

Type: mutation
Input: none
Output: { success: boolean, jobId: string | null }



jobs.runBackup
Enqueue a backup job for one app’s volumes.

Type: mutation
Input: { appName: string, volumes?: string[], retention?: number } — retention defaults to 7 days; omit volumes to back up all of the app’s volumes
Output: { success: boolean, jobId: string | null }







WarningThe backup trait does not schedule anything on its own



Declaring a backup trait emits metadata only — it records schedule and retention and does not create a recurring job. Backups run when something calls this procedure, which requires the control plane to be running. An app with a backup trait and no control plane is not being backed up, and nothing errors to say so.

title: Scope Model Reference
text:
Appbay has two organizational concepts. Each controls a different aspect of how apps are grouped, configured, and deployed.









Concept
Controls
Compose mapping
Cardinality




Namespace
Deployment identity and variable scope
Container, network and edge-fragment names
Single per app


Collection
App selection
Which docker compose up calls are made
Multi per app

Nothing reads projects/<name>/project.yaml or environments/<env>.yaml, so ${{environment.KEY}} and ${{service.KEY}} resolve against empty maps and always fail.
A reference to an unknown key survives the render as a literal and the deploy then refuses the app, so this fails safe — but no error names the missing store directly.

title: Scope Model Reference
text:
Namespace
A namespace is a deployment identity. It distinguishes two instances of the same app in one installation, and it scopes the variables an app resolves against.
# appbay.yaml
namespace: uom.sim
Absence means “decided at deploy time”. The field is optional and has no default, which is what lets a value supplied at compile time take effect — a schema default would shadow it.

What it controls

Container names: appbay.<namespace>.<app>.<service>
The app’s private network: <namespace>_<app>_internal
The shared-network alias other apps dial: <namespace>_<app>_<service>
The generated edge fragment: <namespace>.<app>.caddy / .yml

⚠️ Dots become hyphens wherever the namespace reaches a hostname. A dot separates labels in DNS, so uom.sim_litellm_web would parse as host uom in domain sim_litellm_web and resolve to nothing. An app in namespace uom.sim publishes uom-sim_litellm_web.


An un-namespaced app is unchanged
When namespace: is absent — the case for every shipped manifest — the namespace is omitted from all four names entirely:




no namespace
namespace: uom.sim




container
appbay.litellm.web
appbay.uom-sim.litellm.web


network
litellm_internal
uom-sim_litellm_internal


alias
litellm_web
uom-sim_litellm_web


edge fragment
litellm.caddy
uom-sim.litellm.caddy



This is deliberate: including it unconditionally would rename every container on every existing host in order to disambiguate installations that have nothing to disambiguate.


When to use a namespace

Two instances of one app in one installation (uom.sim and uom.prod)
Separate variable values for the same config keys

title: Scope Model Reference
text:
Collection
A collection is an operational grouping – a named set of apps that are deployed, restarted, or stopped together. Collections are purely a selection mechanism.
# appbay.yaml
collection: [ai-stack, gpu-apps]

What it controls
Which apps are included in a batch operation. Nothing else.


What it does NOT control

Variable values (use environment for that)
Naming prefixes (use project for that)
Network isolation (use project for that)



Multi-valued
An app can belong to multiple collections:
# ollama
collection: [ai-stack, gpu-apps]

# jellyfin
collection: [media, gpu-apps]


CLI usage
appbay up --collection ai-stack          # Deploy all ai-stack apps
appbay up ollama webui                   # Deploy specific apps (no collection needed)
appbay down ollama webui tts             # Stop apps by name
appbay restart ollama jellyfin           # Restart apps by name

title: Scope Model Reference
text:
Variable resolution
Variables are resolved by scope prefix — each ${{scope.KEY}} reference targets exactly one variable store. There is no cascading fallthrough.
Collection is NOT part of variable resolution. It is a selector, not a scope level.

Variable reference syntax








Syntax
Resolves from
Only from




${{project.KEY}}
etc/system.yaml (domain: only)
project store only


${{environment.KEY}}
etc/projects/<name>/environments/<env>.yaml
environment store only


${{service.KEY}}
Service-level vars in appbay.yaml or .env
service store only



Undefined variable references produce explicit errors with the scope and key name. Appbay never silently substitutes empty strings.


Resolution example
# projects/homelab/project.yaml
vars:
  DOMAIN: home.lan
  TZ: UTC

# projects/homelab/environments/prod.yaml
vars:
  DOMAIN: homelab.example.com    # separate environment-scope value, does NOT override project-scope
  TZ: America/New_York
Resolution of ${{project.DOMAIN}} in any environment: - Returns home.lan — resolved from project.yaml only
Resolution of ${{environment.DOMAIN}}: - In prod: returns homelab.example.com — resolved from prod.yaml - In dev (if dev.yaml has no DOMAIN): compile error — undefined variable


Magic generators








Generator
Output
Persisted?




${password:N}
Random N-character password
Yes – stored in generated-values.yaml


${uuid}
Random UUID v4
Yes


${base64:N}
Random N-byte base64 string
Yes


${hash}
Deterministic hash of (project + env + service + key)
No – always reproducible


${timestamp}
Current ISO timestamp
No – evaluated at render time



Generated values are keyed by (project, environment, service, var_name). Once generated, they are reused on subsequent compiles to ensure deterministic output.

title: Scope Model Reference
text:
Compose runtime mapping
When you run appbay up --collection ai-stack:
1. Select apps tagged with collection: ai-stack
   -> [ollama, webui, tts]

2. For each app, resolve variables:
   ${{project.DOMAIN}} from $APPBAY_HOME/etc/system.yaml
   (${{environment.KEY}} and ${{service.KEY}} resolve against empty maps -- see the
    warning at the top of this page)

3. Compile each app:
   upstream transform -> overlays -> traits -> render

4. Execute each app as a separate Compose project:
   docker compose -f renders/ollama/docker-compose.rendered.yml up -d
   docker compose -f renders/webui/docker-compose.rendered.yml up -d
   docker compose -f renders/tts/docker-compose.rendered.yml up -d
Each app is an independent Compose project. They communicate via shared networks (e.g., appbay_shared), not via Compose’s internal service discovery.

text:
Filesystem layout
⚠️ This is the intended layout, not the built one. etc/projects/ is not read by anything — ProjectConfigSchema and EnvironmentConfigSchema exist and have no non-test consumers, and the string "projects" is never joined into a path. The one file that is read is $APPBAY_HOME/etc/system.yaml at the root.
$APPBAY_HOME/
  project.yaml                          # the ONE config that is read; `domain:` -> ${{project.DOMAIN}}
  etc/
    projects/                           # ⚠️ specified, not implemented -- nothing reads this
      homelab/
        project.yaml
        environments/
          prod.yaml
    apps/
      ollama/                           # App definition
        appbay.yaml                     # namespace: uom.sim, collection: [ai-stack]
        docker-compose.yml
      jellyfin/
        appbay.yaml                     # collection: [media]
        docker-compose.yml

title: Scope Model Reference
text:
Anti-patterns

Do not use collections for variable scoping
# WRONG: no collection-level variable resolution exists
# RIGHT: use a namespace, or app-level overrides
namespace: prod


Do not use a namespace for operational grouping
# WRONG -- a namespace is a deployment identity, not a label
namespace: ai-apps
namespace: media-apps

# RIGHT -- group with collections, which are multi-valued
collection: [ai-stack]    # ollama
collection: [media]       # jellyfin


Do not use a namespace to select different app sets
# WRONG -- namespace does not choose which apps deploy
namespace: minimal
namespace: full

# RIGHT -- collections select, the namespace identifies
collection: [core]
collection: [core, extras]
